Straight
strāt
a. (direct, not crooked; in Scripture the condition of the way prepared for the LORD, and of the path a man makes for his own feet)
From Middle English streight, the past participle of strecchen, to stretch — a straight line is a stretched one. It is a different word from strait, meaning narrow, which comes from Latin strictus; the Authorized Version distinguishes them, and the strait gate of Mat 7:13 is the narrow one, not the straight one.

Biblical Definition

Straight is the condition of a road fit for a king, and John the Baptist's whole ministry is described by it. Isaiah gives the commission: “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God” (Isa 40:3), which all four Gospels apply to John (Mat 3:3). The image is of an eastern road party going ahead of a monarch, filling valleys and levelling ridges — and what John actually did was preach repentance, which is the levelling. Hebrews puts the same duty on every believer, and adds a pastoral reason: “make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed” (Heb 12:13) — a man's crooked walking trips the weaker Christians behind him. The Preacher marks the limit of human effort: “That which is crooked cannot be made straight” (Ecc 1:15). And the word survives as a street name in the oldest Christian narrative outside the Gospels: “go into the street which is called Straight, and enquire in the house of Judas for one called Saul, of Tarsus: for, behold, he prayeth” (Act 9:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines straight as right, in a right line, not crooked; and notes that it is distinct from strait, which signifies narrow, though the two are often confounded.

expand to see more

STRAIGHT, a. Right, in a mathematical sense; direct; passing from one point to another by the nearest course.

A straight line is the shortest distance between two points.

2. Narrow; close; tight. [But in this sense strait is now used.]

3. Upright; according with justice and rectitude; not deviating from truth or fairness.

Note. Straight is from stretch; strait, from the Latin strictus, narrow. The words are often confounded.

Key Scripture

Isa 40:3 — "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God."

Mat 3:3 — "For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight."

Heb 12:13 — "And make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed."

Ecc 1:15 — "That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered."

Modern Corruption

“Prepare ye the way” is turned into a slogan for worship atmospherics and revival technique, when John's way of preparing it was to preach repentance and to name particular sins.

expand to see more

Isa 40:3 is regularly invoked to describe stirring a congregation into a receptive frame, or to justify whatever a ministry proposes as preparation for God's moving. The Gospels leave no doubt what preparation looked like when the man commissioned to do it actually did it: John preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, told the multitude to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance, told the publicans to exact no more than was appointed, told the soldiers to do violence to no man and be content with their wages, and told Herod that it was not lawful to have his brother's wife. That last sentence cost him his head. Making the way straight is specific and it is costly.

Ecc 1:15 supplies the limit that keeps the doctrine honest. What is crooked cannot be made straight — not by the man himself. The Preacher is surveying human effort under the sun and finding it unable to correct what is bent, which is exactly the conclusion Romans reaches about the law and the flesh. The straightening in Isaiah is done for God's coming, not by the traveller's own strength, and the levelling John preached was a call to admit crookedness rather than to repair it. Heb 12:13 then gives the believer his actual assignment, which is smaller and more practical: walk straight, because the lame are behind you.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle English streight, stretched; rendering Hebrew yashar (H3474), to be straight or upright, and Greek euthus (G2117), straight, and orthos (G3717), upright.

expand to see more

Middle English streight — past participle of strecchen, to stretch; a straight line is a stretched one.

Hebrew yashar (H3474) — to be straight, level, upright; the same root gives Jeshurun, the upright one, a poetic name for Israel.

Greek euthus (G2117) — straight, direct; “make his paths straight” (Mat 3:3), and the adverb eutheos, straightway.

Greek orthos (G3717) — upright, straight; “make straight paths for your feet” (Heb 12:13), whence English orthodox and orthopaedic.

Distinguish strait — Latin strictus, narrow; the strait gate of Mat 7:13 is narrow, not straight, and the KJV keeps the two words apart.

Usage

"“Make straight in the desert a highway” — and the levelling was preached repentance."

"“Make straight paths for your feet” — because the lame are walking behind you."

"“That which is crooked cannot be made straight” — not by the man himself."
